lead: A rectifier gives DC that still pulses. Ripple is the unwanted AC part left on that DC. A filter reduces ripple by storing energy or by blocking alternating current. The commonest is a capacitor across the load: it charges near the peak and then discharges slowly through the load while the rectifier output falls. An LC section then removes the remaining high-frequency ripple. Every power supply that charges a phone or runs a router uses this idea before a regulator, because a regulator needs a fairly steady input to hold its output clean.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 rectifier waveforms and the RC time constant and impedance.

blocks.text: The capacitor-input filter sits directly after the rectifier. During each pulse, the rectifier output rises. The diode conducts and charges C. C stores charge and its voltage reaches about Vm, the peak rectified voltage. When the pulse falls, the diode turns off. C now supplies the load current through R. Its voltage falls slowly. The next pulse charges C again. This charge-discharge cycle repeats at f: twice per cycle for full-wave, once per cycle for half-wave.

The discharge is set by the time constant RC. A large C or a large R makes the droop small, so the load sees nearly steady DC. The average output is below the peak by about half the peak-to-peak ripple.

items: Rectifier output rises; diode conducts and C charges toward Vm.
Output falls below capacitor voltage; diode turns off.
C discharges through R; load voltage droops.
Next pulse recharges C to near Vm.

blocks.where: Vdc is the average DC output in V; Vm is the peak rectified voltage in V; Vr(pp) is the peak-to-peak ripple voltage in V.

blocks.text: During discharge, load current is about I = Vdc/R. The capacitor loses charge ΔQ = I × Δt. For full-wave, the discharge time is about 1/(2f); for half-wave it is 1/f. Since Vr(pp) = ΔQ/C, the approximate formulas follow. They assume small ripple, Vr(pp) much less than Vdc, and steady load current.
Full-wave: Vr(pp) ≈ Vdc/(2fCR). Half-wave: Vr(pp) ≈ Vdc/(fCR).
blocks.where: f is supply frequency in Hz; C is filter capacitance in farad; R is load resistance in ohm; Vdc is average DC in V; Vr(pp) is peak-to-peak ripple in V.

blocks.text: Ripple factor compares the AC part with the DC part. Use rms values: r = Vr(rms)/Vdc. A sawtooth-like ripple has Vr(rms) = Vr(pp)/(2√3). So r ≈ 1/(4√3 fCR) for full-wave and 1/(2√3 fCR) for half-wave. Some notes quote the peak ratio Vr(pp)/Vdc and call it ripple factor; in an exam, state which definition you use.

A single capacitor is a first-order filter. Its shunt impedance at ripple frequency is 1/(2πfC). A series resistor and shunt capacitor form an RC low-pass filter. Above cut-off, gain falls about 20 dB per decade. The resistor also drops DC voltage, so an RC filter wastes power in a supply.

An LC section uses a series inductor and shunt capacitor. The inductor blocks high-frequency ripple and the capacitor bypasses it. Above its natural frequency, a simple LC low-pass falls about 40 dB per decade. RLC adds damping and avoids a sharp resonance peak. Some syllabi call these passive filters. Active filters, including Gm-C filters, are in Unit 7. A regulator in Chapter 1.4 or Chapter 1.5 needs this clean DC.
RC cut-off: fc = 1/(2πRC). LC natural frequency: f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)).
blocks.where: R is series resistance in ohm; C is capacitance in farad; L is inductance in henry; fc and f0 are in Hz. Exact LC cut-off also depends on source and load.

figure.caption: The capacitor charges near the peak, then holds the load voltage while it discharges. The LC section removes the remaining high-frequency ripple.

examples.question: A full-wave bridge rectifier with Vm = 12 V, f = 50 Hz feeds a capacitor C = 1000 µF and load R = 100 Ω. Use the approximate capacitor-filter formulas and ideal diodes. Find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage, the DC output and the rms ripple factor.
steps: DC output: Vdc ≈ Vm − Vr(pp)/2 = 12 V − Vdc/20. Thus 1.05 Vdc = 12 V, giving Vdc = 11.43 V.
rms ripple: Vr(rms) = Vr(pp)/(2√3) = 1.14 V / 3.464 = 0.330 V.
Ripple factor: r = Vr(rms)/Vdc = 0.330 V / 11.43 V = 0.0289.
examples.answer: The peak-to-peak ripple is 1.14 V, the DC output is 11.43 V, and the rms ripple factor is 0.0289 (2.89%); the peak ratio is 0.10. A real bridge subtracts about 1.4 V of diode drop, which lowers Vdc but leaves this ripple-factor formula almost unchanged.
examples.check:
import math
Vm=12.0
f=50.0
C=1000e-6
R=100.0
k=2*f*C*R
Vdc=Vm/(1+1/(2*k))
Vr=Vdc/k
rms=Vr/(2*math.sqrt(3))
r=rms/Vdc
peak=Vr/Vdc
print(f'{Vr:.2f}')
print(f'{Vdc:.2f}')
print(f'{r:.4f}')
print(f'{peak:.2f}')

traps: Full-wave has two pulses per cycle. Use 2fCR, not fCR, in the ripple formula.
Ripple factor uses rms ripple. Vr(pp)/Vdc is the peak ratio; divide by 2√3 for the true ripple factor.
A real bridge has two diode drops. Subtract about 1.4 V from Vm before finding Vdc; otherwise Vdc is high by about 1.4 V.
The capacitor formulas assume Vr(pp) much less than Vdc and steady load current. At heavy load, small C or small R, the droop is large and the formulas fail.
Do not mix RC cut-off 1/(2πRC) with LC natural frequency 1/(2π√(LC)); exact LC cut-off also depends on source and load.

quiz.a: r = Vr(rms)/Vdc. Ideal smooth DC has r = 0.

quiz.q: Why does a large capacitor reduce ripple?
quiz.a: It stores more charge. The RC discharge is slower, so the load voltage droops less before the next pulse.

quiz.q: A full-wave filter has Vdc = 15 V, f = 50 Hz, C = 470 µF and R = 220 Ω. Find Vr(pp).
A half-wave filter has Vdc = 9 V, f = 50 Hz, C = 1000 µF and R = 100 Ω. Find Vr(pp).
Why can the capacitor formula fail at high load current?
quiz.a: Small R discharges C fast. Ripple becomes a large part of Vdc, so Vr(pp) much less than Vdc fails. Diode conduction angle also increases.

quiz.q: What does an LC section add after the capacitor?
quiz.a: Series L blocks high-frequency ripple; shunt C bypasses it. It gives a second-order low-pass with steeper attenuation.

quiz.q: What happens if you double C in a capacitor filter?
quiz.a: Approximate ripple halves and Vdc rises slightly. Surge current and diode stress at switch-on increase.

quiz.q: Write the cut-off frequency of an RC low-pass filter.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real supplies the capacitor equivalent series resistance and diode surge current limit how large C can be. Designers use simulation and measured ripple rather than only the hand formula. LC filters need damping because resonance can amplify a ripple harmonic. Gm-C filters replace bulky inductors with active transconductors; they are active filters, so Unit 7 is their place.
